question: As the owner whose close bar promises offline is safe by policy, I want to know whether that promise holds before I attest it. With no production code changed, a high-value must-verify-online code is still offered the offline override whenever the campaign data has not arrived yet. Merging is not in doubt. Does close-bar leg 3 stay attestable, or does it block on a fix?
proposal: Merge, file the gap, and block close-bar leg 3 until it is closed; author the unblocking card at triage

votes.note: Leg 3 IS the offline-safety promise. Signing it while a first-sync window leaves high-value codes overridable would close the milestone on a claim the owner would not make if shown the reproduction. This is the acceptance criterion itself, not a defect under it.

Blocking leg 3 costs one card and moves the close out; promoting the fix ahead of Activity 0 would cost more, because Activity 0 carries the longest external lead times and is the real critical path. Authoring the unblocking card at triage keeps the block from being a dead end.

Cheap to reproduce and cheap to guard: the regression test already exists in shape — the shipped branch-3 e2e with its campaigns seed removed. The fix is a readiness gate or a fail-closed default, both small. The card is still a strict improvement on a refusal that was previously unreachable, so nothing argues against merging.

cited.statement: Red-first evidence is a named gate row in the ladder — a card that has not shown its red cannot merge. An obligation that matters gets a gate, not a reminder in a launch prompt.
cited.fit: Red-first is a gate, not a memory test — the reproduction was produced by running the shipped test with one seed line removed and zero production mutation, which is what makes this a defect rather than a reading of the code. The same standard is what the unblocking card's done_when now demands: red before, green after.

cited.statement: before closing anything under P-3, state the condition you sampled — load, concurrency, data volume, journal depth — and whether it is the condition the original report described. *"Could not reproduce on a quiet box"* is a finding; *"could not reproduce"* is not. Absence of reproduction in N legs bounds a rate conditional on the sampled condition only.
cited.weight: strong — this is the corollary that makes P-3 safe to apply; applying P-3 without it is how a live bug gets closed.
cited.fit: A reproduction attempt must sample the RIGHT condition or it proves nothing — the run measured the adjacent case (no policy source at all) and generalised to the whole class, missing the case where the code replicated and its campaign did not. That is exactly the wrong-condition failure, and it is why an APPROVE verdict coexisted with an open hole.

weighing: Both cited preferences bear on the finding rather than on the timing, and both were honored: gates/P-1 is why the gap counts as reproduced fact, process/P-4 is why the run's own measurement did not rule it out. Neither speaks to whether the operator should hold their close bar, which is a judgment about their own acceptance criterion and nobody else's — so the question was escalated rather than auto-resolved, and the escalation is the correct disposition.
reasons: top-severity questions are the operator's — no number of citations clears them

question: The owner previously agreed that a code from a campaign nobody has heard of may be overridden offline. Does that agreement also cover a high-value code the device is holding, whose campaign data simply has not arrived yet? Reading it broadly would make the new gap already-permitted; reading it narrowly makes it an open defect.
proposal: Rule the unreplicated-campaign case outside the earlier agreement and treat it as an open defect

votes.note: The owner said yes to a policy about codes nobody has heard of. They were never shown a $40 code the tablet is holding with its campaign missing. Stretching the yes to cover that converts a narrow permission into cover for a failure mode they never saw.

The broad reading is the one a future reader will reach for, because it is available in writing and it closes the finding for free. Recording the narrow ruling now is what stops the gap being quietly absorbed at the next planning round.

The two cases are distinguishable in the data, not just in intent: one has no code row and no campaign row, the other has a replicated, entitlement-bearing code row and a missing campaign row. A guard can tell them apart, so treating them as one class is a choice rather than a constraint.

cited.statement: A decision number, backlog handle, ledger section, card ID, key-result name, gate label or commit SHA carries no meaning on its own. Attach what it identifies, in a few words, on first use in any document or message — "decision 126 (reads move to RxDB, writes stay on REST)", not "decision 126". Keep the identifier; never let it travel alone. This binds the written record too: the ledger, handoffs and commit bodies are where bare numbers accumulate and are hardest to decode later, because nobody reads a ledger linearly. A short gloss beats a perfect one.
cited.fit: Never cite an identifier without the thing it identifies — citing the earlier ratification by its number to excuse this case is exactly that failure: the number carries a scope the citation would silently widen. Naming what was actually ratified, in the words it was ratified in, is what shows it does not reach here.

cited.statement: before closing anything under P-3, state the condition you sampled — load, concurrency, data volume, journal depth — and whether it is the condition the original report described. *"Could not reproduce on a quiet box"* is a finding; *"could not reproduce"* is not. Absence of reproduction in N legs bounds a rate conditional on the sampled condition only.
cited.weight: strong — this is the corollary that makes P-3 safe to apply; applying P-3 without it is how a live bug gets closed.
cited.fit: A reproduction attempt must sample the RIGHT condition — the run's measurement sampled the no-policy-source condition and the ratification sampled the unknown-code condition; neither sampled a known code with an unreplicated campaign, so neither can speak to it.

weighing: process/P-5 does the decisive work: the temptation here is a citation that widens the operator's own scope by reference rather than by argument, and refusing that is what keeps a ratification meaningful. process/P-4 supplies the supporting fact that no existing measurement covers the case. Both point the same way and the ruling is interpretive rather than a product fork, so it resolved at role level; the operator's separate call on whether to block leg 3 was escalated on its own.

question: The night reported its test failures as one already-known flaky test plus load noise. Running the same suite on a clean baseline with none of the night's changes gives a different set of failures, and the test the night named as the known one passed every way it was tried. Do we accept the night's account because its safety conclusion was right, or require the known-failure list to be re-derived before it is cited again?
proposal: File it and require re-derivation before the named baseline failure is cited again

votes.note: Nothing here changes whether the night's work was safe — it was, and independently so. What it changes is whether the team can tell a new breakage from an old one next time, which is the only reason the known-failure list exists.

This fails silently and in the reassuring direction: a wrong name on the list makes everything look already-known. Left alone it degrades every future night's report, so the cost of not filing compounds while the cost of filing is one backlog entry.

Measured, not inferred: the baseline run gives 856 passed / 4 failed / 6 skipped, the named test passed at whole-suite position, in isolation and in file order, and three of the four real failures sit in one spec file the night never mentioned. None is attributable to the night's changes.

cited.statement: before closing anything under P-3, state the condition you sampled — load, concurrency, data volume, journal depth — and whether it is the condition the original report described. *"Could not reproduce on a quiet box"* is a finding; *"could not reproduce"* is not. Absence of reproduction in N legs bounds a rate conditional on the sampled condition only.
cited.weight: strong — this is the corollary that makes P-3 safe to apply; applying P-3 without it is how a live bug gets closed.
cited.fit: A reproduction attempt must sample the RIGHT condition or it proves nothing — the night inferred a baseline property from runs that all carried its own changes; the only sample that can establish it is a run on the untouched baseline, which is what triage did and what produced the contradiction.

cited.statement: any flake, intermittent failure, or defect report that survives a genuine reproduction attempt without reproducing is closed — and reopened without embarrassment if it recurs. Closing it records what was attempted, under what conditions, and what failure rate the attempt bounds. Distinguish *"not flaky"* (no mechanism, no reproduction — close it) from *"rare, mechanism understood, bounded at N%"* (a real mechanism firing rarely), and never launder the second into the first.
cited.weight: strong — a default that requires a stated reason to depart from, not an absolute rule.
cited.fit: Unreproducible means resolved, until it recurs — read loosely this argues for letting the named failure go, since it did not reproduce. It is cited against the proposal so the tension is on the record: it does not apply here, because the claim being tested is that the failure is a KNOWN BASELINE, and a non-reproduction falsifies that claim rather than retiring the failure.

weighing: process/P-4 carries it: the night's characterisation rested on samples that could not establish the property it asserted. process/P-3 is cited against on purpose — it is the preference most likely to be reached for here, and reaching for it would invert its meaning, retiring a label's SUBJECT on the strength of evidence that falsifies the LABEL. Recording the tension is the point; the ruling is that a non-reproduction of a claimed baseline is a finding about the claim, not a retirement of the test.
reasons: top-severity questions are the operator's — no number of citations clears them
cited preferences conflict at equal strength (strong for, strong against) — the decree does not resolve this on weight alone
